summary.text: An Arcadian virgin huntress who joined the chiefs against the Calydonian boar and drew first blood, for which Meleager awarded her the hide.
Her parentage is disputed: Apollodorus calls her daughter of Iasus by Clymene, exposed at birth and suckled by a she-bear, while elsewhere he and Hyginus name her daughter of Schoeneus.

story.text: When Oeneus gathered the chiefs to hunt the great boar of Calydon, Atalanta, daughter of Schoeneus, came from Arcadia and was the first to strike the beast, shooting it in the back with an arrow. After it was slain Meleager gave its hide to her; but when the sons of Thestius, his uncles, tried to take it away he killed them, and so was destroyed himself.

Ovid sets her at the hunt as the virgin of Mount Lycaeus, glory of her sex, an Arcadian with a bow in her hand. It was her arrow that quivered beneath the monster's ear and reddened its hard bristles with the first blood, and Meleager, taken with her, hailed her for the honor of that wound.

In another account Apollodorus calls her the daughter of Iasus by Clymene, exposed by her father because he wanted male children; a she-bear came again and again to give her suck until hunters reared her, and she grew up a virgin who kept always under arms in the wilderness.
Hyginus too tells of Atalanta, the most beautiful daughter of Schoeneus, who by her swiftness used to outrun men in the race.

Apollonius records that she longed to sail on the Argo and gave Jason a spear as a guest-gift when she met him in Maenalus, but he himself kept her from the quest, fearing bitter strife on account of her love; so she was named among the would-be Argonauts yet excluded from the crew.
